intro: Florence was built on rivalries: between guilds, between families, between architects competing to leave their mark on the very same square. Every dome, every statue and every tower on this route is, deep down, the answer to a challenge. It's about 1.5 km through the heart of the Renaissance.
puntoPartida: Piazza del Duomo, facing the façade of Santa Maria del Fiore

paradas.titulo: The façade that pretends to be medieval
paradas.llegada: Standing in Piazza del Duomo, look at the cathedral's main façade: white, green and pink marble forming a geometric pattern.
paradas.enigma: This façade looks medieval, matching the rest of the Gothic building — but it's actually from the 19th century, completed in 1887. Look closely at the marble pattern: how many different marble colours make up the façade's geometric design?
pistas: The colours are white, green and one more.
The third colour resembles a pinkish or reddish semi-precious stone.
There are three colours: white, green and pink/red.
paradas.historia: The design is by Emilio De Fabris, who died in 1883 without seeing his work completed. The cathedral's original Gothic façade was left unfinished in the 16th century and stayed that way, bare, for nearly 300 years, until Florence decided to complete it in 19th-century neo-Gothic taste — at almost the same time, incidentally, that Barcelona was doing the same thing to its own cathedral.
paradas.fuente: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore; Comune di Firenze

paradas.llegada: Walk around the building until you get a good view of the great red dome crowning the cathedral.
paradas.enigma: Filippo Brunelleschi built this dome between 1420 and 1436 without using the standard method of the time for supporting stone while it's being built. What did Brunelleschi NOT use to raise the dome, unlike almost any other similar construction of his era?
pistas: It's a temporary wooden structure that holds stone in place while the mortar sets.
Without it, any architect of the time would have called the dome impossible.
He did not use wooden scaffolding (centering).
paradas.historia: Brunelleschi invented a system of brick rings arranged in a "herringbone" pattern that supported themselves as they rose. At 45.5 metres in internal diameter, it remains the largest unreinforced brick dome ever built — a record that has stood for almost 600 years.
paradas.fuente: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore — Cupola del Brunelleschi

paradas.llegada: Walk to the Battistero di San Giovanni, the octagonal building facing the cathedral, and find the east door, the one facing the main façade.
paradas.enigma: This gilded bronze door was made by Lorenzo Ghiberti between 1425 and 1452, and an even more famous artist gave it the nickname it's known by today. Count the square panels that make up the door, each showing a scene from the Old Testament.
pistas: Ghiberti had planned many more panels, but cut the number in half to make each one bigger and more detailed.
It's five rows of two panels each.
There are 10 panels.
paradas.historia: It was Michelangelo who, upon seeing it, nicknamed it "the Gate of Paradise" — a name that has stuck forever. The original panels, damaged in a 1966 flood, are now kept safe at the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo; what you see on the door are exact copies.
paradas.fuente: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore — Porta del Paradiso

paradas.titulo: The tower its namesake never finished
paradas.llegada: Now find the tall, multicoloured marble bell tower next to the cathedral, the Campanile.
paradas.enigma: This bell tower bears the name of the artist who designed it and began building it in 1334. But he wasn't the one who finished it: a plague epidemic interrupted the work, and another architect completed it in 1359, after continuing the efforts of a third master in between. Who gives the tower its name, even though he never saw it finished?
pistas: He's better known as a painter than as an architect.
He's one of the great names of Italian art right before the Renaissance.
The tower is called the Campanile di Giotto.
paradas.historia: Giotto only built the first levels before dying in 1337. Andrea Pisano continued the work, and it was finally Francesco Talenti who completed it in 1359. The 414 steps to the terrace climb 84.7 metres — and the white, green and red marble cladding is the same you'll see repeated on the cathedral and the baptistery: all three buildings share the same language of stone.
paradas.fuente: Opera di Santa Maria del Fiore — Campanile di Giotto

paradas.titulo: The giant that isn't the original
paradas.llegada: Walk to Piazza della Signoria and find the great statue of a nude standing man, right in front of the entrance to Palazzo Vecchio.
paradas.enigma: This statue depicts David, Michelangelo's masterpiece. But what's in front of you isn't the original: it's a copy installed in 1910. Where is the authentic David kept, moved there in 1873 for its protection?
pistas: It's a museum, not another open-air square.
It's largely dedicated to Michelangelo himself.
The original is at the Galleria dell'Accademia.
paradas.historia: For over 350 years, the original David stood exposed to the elements right here, until deterioration forced its move indoors. There's now even a third version, in bronze, at the Piazzale Michelangelo — so Florence has, in total, three different Davids scattered around the city.
paradas.fuente: Musei del Bargello; Comune di Firenze

paradas.titulo: The four figures at the hero's feet
paradas.llegada: Right next door, under the great arches of the Loggia dei Lanzi, find the bronze statue of a man holding a severed head.
paradas.enigma: This is Benvenuto Cellini's Perseus (1545-1554), holding Medusa's head. On the statue's marble base there are several smaller bronze figures placed in niches. Count how many figures are on that base.
pistas: They're gods and figures from classical mythology, much smaller than Perseus himself.
It's an even number, between 2 and 6.
There are 4 figures: Mercury, Minerva, Jupiter and Danaë.
paradas.historia: Cellini, a goldsmith before he was a sculptor, took nine years to cast this piece in bronze, using a technique so risky it nearly failed completely on the night of the final pour. The whole Loggia works almost as an open-air sculpture museum — free, open day and night, right in the heart of the city.

paradas.titulo: The two ways of defending a city
paradas.llegada: Look up at the Torre di Arnolfo, the tall crenellated tower of Palazzo Vecchio.
paradas.enigma: Look closely at the battlements crowning the wall and tower: they don't all have the same shape. Some are square, and others end in a double point, like a swallow's tail — each shape identified a rival political faction in medieval Florence. How many different battlement shapes can you make out?
pistas: One is simple and rectangular; the other has a V-shaped notch at the tip.
They represented the two opposing factions: Guelphs and Ghibellines.
There are two different battlement shapes.
paradas.historia: Square battlements (Guelph) and swallow-tail ones (Ghibelline) marked, at a glance, all over Italy, which side a building belonged to: the Guelphs supported the Pope, the Ghibellines the Holy Roman Emperor. The tower's great clock, from 1667, still works today with its original mechanism.

paradas.titulo: The bridge that no longer smells of meat
paradas.llegada: Finish by walking to the Ponte Vecchio, the medieval bridge covered in small shops, and find the bronze bust halfway across.
paradas.enigma: This bridge was full of butcher shops for centuries, until a grand duke, fed up with the stench beneath his private elevated passage, ordered them replaced with a far nobler trade in 1593. The bust you see on the bridge depicts the most celebrated Florentine goldsmith of all. What trade did — and still do — almost all the shops on the bridge practise?
pistas: They work with gold, silver and precious stones.
The bridge's bust depicts one of them, also the sculptor of the Perseus you've already seen.
They're goldsmiths and jewellers.
paradas.historia: The bust is of Benvenuto Cellini, placed in 1901 for the fourth centenary of his birth — the same sculptor behind the Perseus at the Loggia dei Lanzi. Above the shops runs, invisible from here, the Vasari Corridor: an elevated passage nearly a kilometre long that let the Medici cross from one palace to another without ever setting foot on the street.

final.titulo: You've watched Florence compete with itself
final.texto: From a façade pretending to be 600 years old to a dome built without scaffolding, from a door nicknamed by Michelangelo to a David that's only a copy, all the way to a bridge that changed its smell by decree. Florence was built competing with itself, generation after generation — and the result is the city you've just walked through.
